threats.name: Use After Free
threats.rationale: Use after free needs manual deallocation. The JVM frees an object only when it is unreachable, so a live reference never dangles. Kotlin/JVM code runs on a garbage-collected, bounds-checked runtime. The residual routes are native memory (an `external` function, JNI, Unsafe, the foreign-memory API, or Kotlin/Native interop), none of which the library uses: LogicGates.kt has no `external` declaration and no import statement (default imports such as java.lang.* are still in scope, so the FFI analyzer rule must resolve names).

closed_by.detail: No `external` function, no System.load/loadLibrary, no sun.misc.Unsafe, jdk.internal.misc, java.lang.foreign, MethodHandles or JNI/JNA use, and no Kotlin/Native cinterop or @CName, in the library sources. The rule resolves names, not just import lines: java.lang.* and kotlin.* are default-imported, so `System.load(...)` needs no import statement.

The JVM verifies bytecode, bounds-checks every array index, null-checks dereferences and has no pointer arithmetic or manual free; a memory error in pure Kotlin/JVM code surfaces as an exception, not corruption. A statement about the runtime, not a check on the package; it holds only while no JNI, Unsafe or foreign-memory use exists (the FFI analyzer rule).

threats.name: NULL Pointer Dereference
threats.rationale: The JVM turns every null dereference into an exception instead of memory corruption, and Kotlin's non-null types stop a Kotlin caller from passing null at all: the eleven basic gates take primitive Int. The residual route is a Java caller. Verified in this review by compiling the package at origin/main 7a793727a16 and calling it from a Java class: LogicGates.INSTANCE.AND_N((int[]) null) and XOR_N((int[]) null) throw java.lang.NullPointerException, raised by the compiler-generated Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter at the top of every N-ary gate (javap shows it at offset 3). So null does not corrupt anything, but the error is a NullPointerException, not the package's documented IllegalArgumentException family (LogicGates.kt:438, 456, 482), and no test passes a null array because the tests are written in Kotlin. The registry subset gc_runtimes does not close the class on its own: the null is reachable from public input. A boxed `Integer` null passed to NOT/AND... NPEs in the CALLER at the unboxing, before the library runs (kotlin.null-unboxing-at-java-call-site).

closed_by.detail: Flow analysis shows no public function dereferences a reference-typed parameter that may be null; a Java-callable vararg IntArray must be guarded explicitly (or the module must keep the compiler-generated check and the contract must name its exception).

threats.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
threats.rationale: The two-input gates do constant work. The N-ary gates do linear work in an array the CALLER already holds, with no cap on main. Verified with javap in this review: XOR_N builds the name `"bit[$i]"` EAGERLY for every element on every call (an invokedynamic string concatenation before the call to validateBit, LogicGates.kt:485), so a successful XOR_N over n elements allocates n short Strings, a per-call allocation proportional to input that the success path never uses. Each rejection also constructs an exception and fills its stack trace, a cost per rejected call that a caller feeding invalid input in a loop pays. Kotlin callers pass the array through the spread operator, which copies it. Both causes are fixable inside the package: a length cap plus a name built only on failure. LGE-KT-NARY (local branch) caps the length at 65,536 and snapshots the array (LogicGates.kt:431-459 on that branch) and builds "inputs[$i]" lazily (NaryGatesTest.kt:47-58 tests the boundary). The registry route pure_zero_allocation is the closest subset; the closing rules are the planned loop-bound analyzer rule and the N-ary rows. The registry's discharge evidence (microbenchmark, step-bound proof, input-bound check) cannot all be supplied, so there is no discharge route.

threats.name: Concurrent Execution Race Condition
threats.rationale: The library has no shared state of its own: `object LogicGates` declares no property, and class initialisation is serialized by the JVM. No Thread, coroutine, lock or lazy delegate is used. The one concurrency hazard is the caller's array. Kotlin differs from Java here. A Kotlin caller must write the spread operator (`AND_N(*arr)`), and spreading COPIES the array, so a Kotlin caller cannot alias its array into the gate. A Java caller passes its int[] directly (`LogicGates.INSTANCE.XOR_N(arr)`), so the callee sees the live array. XOR_N validates every element in one loop (LogicGates.kt:485) and then re-reads `bits[0]` and `bits[i]` (:487-490); a second thread mutating the array between the loops makes a value that was validated as 0 or 1 be read as something else, and XOR(result, 7) then raises InvalidBitException from the 2-input gate under the wrong name. AND_N and OR_N read each element once through AND/OR, so they have no check-then-reread window.

threats.name: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition
threats.rationale: The classic file TOCTOU does not apply (no file access). The structural twin does: XOR_N checks the whole caller array and then uses it again. Kotlin differs from Java here. A Kotlin caller must write the spread operator (`AND_N(*arr)`), and spreading COPIES the array, so a Kotlin caller cannot alias its array into the gate. AND_N and OR_N read each element once through AND/OR, so they have no check-then-reread window.
